Development of suction monitoring systems for evaluating the behaviour of partially saturated soils
Many geotechnical infrastructures are located above the groundwater level, making the soils in these areas unsaturated. However, their design and analysis are often based on the assumption of saturated soil conditions. This approach overlooks critical behavioural characteristics of unsaturated soils that can cause significant problems, particularly in the context of climate impacts on infrastructure. Examples include soil swelling and shrinkage due to moisture variations, collapse upon wetting, and failure caused by suction loss. While unsaturated soil behaviour is more representative of real-world conditions in many geotechnical infrastructure and is directly responsible for the above-mentioned issues, it has not been adequately integrated into geotechnical design protocols. This is primarily due to the complexities and time-intensive nature of laboratory testing required to measure the unsaturated characteristics of soils experimentally.
Soil suction is a key factor influencing the behaviour and stability of unsaturated soils, affecting their permeability, compressibility, and shear strength, all of which are critical for geotechnical applications. While tensiometers are commonly used to measure soil suction in both laboratory and field settings, their limited measurement range and design restrict their application to specific soil types and engineering scenarios. This
project aims to address these limitations by developing a high-capacity tensiometer with enhanced measurement capabilities. The advanced tensiometer will be integrated into various testing setups to enable the accurate measurement of soil suction in partially saturated soils, facilitating the analysis of their hydraulic and mechanical behaviour varying environmental conditions. The findings will contribute to the development of improved testing protocols, simplifying the analysis and characterisation of unsaturated soils and enhancing the design of geotechnical infrastructure based on Unsaturated Soil Mechanics.

Resilient Modulus of Road and Railway Subgrades under Seasonal Moisture Variations: Integrating Suction-Dependent Behaviour and Machine Learning Approaches
Resilient Modulus of Road and Railway Subgrades under Seasonal Moisture Variations: Integrating Suction-Dependent Behaviour and Machine Learning Approaches
The resilient modulus (Mr) of road and railway subgrades is a key parameter governing long-term performance under repeated traffic loading. Seasonal wetting and drying cycles, intensified by climate change, produce significant variations in soil moisture content and matric suction, which directly affect the stiffness and resilient response of geomaterials. These moisture-driven fluctuations can accelerate deterioration and reduce the reliability of transport infrastructure. Yet, existing predictive models frequently struggle to capture such behaviour accurately.
Most established models treat moisture effects implicitly or rely on simplified empirical terms that do not properly account for unsaturated soil behaviour. Matric suction, degree of saturation, and water retention characteristics are rarely incorporated, despite their well-documented influence on the mechanical response of soils. Moreover, natural geomaterials used in transport infrastructure are highly heterogeneous. They vary widely in mineralogy, grain size distribution, plasticity, and structure - factors that introduce variability that traditional models are not designed to handle. These mechanisms create a modelling challenge that classical constitutive frameworks often fail to resolve.
This research aims to improve the prediction of resilient modulus under realistic seasonal moisture variations by integrating suction-dependent unsaturated soil mechanics with modern machine learning (ML) approaches. The objectives are to quantify moisture and suction effects on resilient modulus across representative soil types; evaluate the limitations of existing suction-dependent constitutive models; identify the challenges posed by soil heterogeneity and by behavioural differences between fine and coarse soils; and develop ML models capable of capturing these complex, nonlinear patterns.
The methodology involves first applying established predictive models, including those incorporating suction stress and moisture-dependent stiffness, to experimental datasets available in the literature. Their performance will be evaluated to identify sources of error and the soil conditions under which they fail. Subsequently, a suite of ML models will be trained on to combine existing predictive models and the compiled datasets. These models will incorporate a wide range of soil properties: moisture content, suction, void ratio, gradation, plasticity, and stress conditions to capture the full behavioural complexity. By learning from both models and data, they will overcome the limitations of conventional approaches. Their accuracy, robustness, and generalisability will be compared directly with mechanistic empirical models.
The expected outcome of this research is a ML-supported framework for predicting resilient modulus under seasonally varying moisture conditions. The findings have the potential to enhance road and railway design, reduce maintenance costs, and improve infrastructure resilience in response to changing climatic conditions.
